newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egyptian gov't sees stocks staying strong in '97.
newsitem.headline: Egyptian gov't sees stocks staying strong in '97.

text.p: The Egyptian government's voice to international investors predicted on Thursday that Egyptian share prices in 1997 would show strong gains, continuing the bull run of the last few months, but level off late in 1997.

Youssef Boutros-Ghali, minister of state for economic affairs, told a conference on the financial sector that he expected the market to rise as it did in 1996, though prices of stocks would start to level off late in the year.

"The market index has picked up something like 82 percent from January to January (1996). I expect roughly a repeat performance in 1997. It will be a much bumpier road but on average a repeat performance," he said.

"I expect this year not only to maintain the capital inflows, but to substantially increase them on last year, when we achieved about $700 million in portfolio flows. I expect the economy to about double this number this year -- this should keep the market buoyant," he added. His forecast was in sharp contrast to those of some other conference speakers, who see an early correction and possibly some capital outflow.
The ING Barings specialist on the Egyptian market said on Wednesday he expected a big correction soon and would advise investors to take profits on some of their Egyptian stock now.

Angus Blair, head of the investment bank's Middle East and North Africa division, said the recent price rises made Egypt one of the most expensive emerging markets in the world and only strong growth in corporate earnings this spring could prevent what he called "a mild crisis of confidence."
Boutros-Ghali disagreed. "Price/earnings ratios are between 16 and 17,...a little below where it should be for this kind of market, this kind of economy, this kind of country," he said.

"A lot of people are worried that the market has been moving up too fast, but it has to keep up with the perception (of the transformation in the Egyptian economy) and I think it is only moving as fast as that perception is moving," he added.
The minister said the government would press on with privatization and this should also keep the market buoyant.

"A slowdown, not a correction, is inevitable eventually, around the end of this year, and large market capitalizations (big companies) will slow down a little earlier; smaller market caps will continue generating interest and will probably catch up with the rest of the market," he said.
"In summary, expect a pleasant ride for '97. Hold on to your seats, it may be bumpy in some passages, but overall it will be very pleasant," he concluded.
